chapter_title: Chương 297: Đại ca kiếm hoa hồng khi làm việc

segments.title: Chương 297: Đại ca kiếm hoa hồng khi làm việc
segments.content:
Chen Guiliang took a cursory look at the opinion leaders who were attacking *Age of the Future*.

It was one thing not to look, but quite another to see so many familiar faces.

And these guys weren't direct with their criticism, nor did they mention Chen Guiliang or the game's name. Their articles were masters of sarcastic innuendo.

For example, this piece from Wu Yue San Ren:

"Around the Spring Festival, another 'conscientious domestic' game was released. I won't mention the name; suffice it to say many netizens are discussing it. They claim that after one year and eight months of meticulous work, they've only managed to create the novice village. A friend of mine is a closed beta player, and when I visited him during the New Year, I was truly shocked by this game..."

"The graphics, well, they're quite polished. The opening cinematic is also very dramatic. Are they trying to imitate Blizzard? The various classes, skills, dungeons, fatigue points, and revival coins... why do they all look so familiar? Oh, isn't this the Korean game *DNF*?"

"Many friends in China probably haven't heard of *DNF*. This game was developed by a small Korean company. They were serious about creating something original, so much so that they didn't even have enough for a marketing budget. It fought its way into the top three most-played games in Korean internet cafes on word-of-mouth alone. Hey, they're still in talks for a Chinese publisher, and in a blink, it's been ripped off by our own people!"

"We have a nice term for it now, called 'micro-innovation.' Change the game's story, redo the graphics, and it becomes an independently developed, high-quality domestic product... They can't even copy it right, only managing to copy the novice village map in a year and eight months."

"Think about Blizzard. The dungeon design for *World of Warcraft* alone can spark countless discussions and studies globally. That is true innovation, true meticulous craftsmanship. And look at our Eastern neighbor, who has always had a spirit of craftsmanship, the essence of those classic side-scrolling games..."

"This makes me wonder: why is it so difficult for truly original works to be born in this ancient land of ours? Is the soil not fertile enough? Or is the trend of chasing quick success and instant benefits too prevalent? Or is it that, in our very bones, we lack a certain reverence for originality? Plagiarism, cloaked in the grand guise of micro-innovation, can actually win the praise of the majority of netizens..."

"What about those explorers who are quietly toiling away in corners, trying to forge new paths? Won't their hearts turn cold? When these clever products of micro-innovation flood the Chinese online game market, are we getting closer to or further from becoming a true gaming powerhouse?"

After reading the article, Chen Guiliang couldn't help but sigh in admiration: Well written, with a lofty purpose, profound reflection, and truly thought-provoking! An article of this quality must be quite expensive, right?

In the comment section of this blog post, some netizens proactively tried to explain on Chen Guiliang's behalf, but many more were sneering, mocking, or even cursing.

Many other netizens asked what game it was. After finding out, they too joined the ranks of mockery and verbal abuse.

Someone even said they had misjudged Chen Guiliang. They said *Sanguosha* and *Plants vs. Zombies* were very fun, and they thought Chen Guiliang could create even better games, but now he was just blatantly copying a Korean online game.

Someone else replied, saying that *Sanguosha* was a copy, and Chen Guiliang had always been a copycat.

Chen Guiliang thought to himself: I'll admit that *Sanguosha* is a copy, but it's a copy of a domestic inventor's work. As for *Age of the Future*, I really did make this one myself.

Qu Guohao stood beside Chen Guiliang, staring at the computer screen and said, "Who is this person? Why are his readership and comment numbers so high?"

"A public intellectual. Look at his article, so concerned about the country and its people. Criticizing us is just a side note," Chen Guiliang said with a smile.

This public intellectual graduated from the Beijing University of Technology and had worked at companies like Siemens in Beijing.

After accumulating enough popularity on Tianya, this public intellectual was invited to join Sina Blog. He also wrote for other print media and websites, and his articles were often featured on the homepages of major web portals.

That salary from a foreign enterprise was nothing. He had quit his job two months ago to become a freelance writer.

Well, he later immigrated to Japan and even claimed that nuclear wastewater was healthy.

An even more incredible move was when his wife was on her deathbed, he went off to celebrate his mistress's birthday. After his wife died, he wrote a sentimental article mourning her deeply, moving unsuspecting netizens to tears.

These well-known opinion leaders had truly powerful influence and a strong ability to incite others.

Chen Guiliang originally had an excellent reputation online, but because of one or two articles from those guys, many netizens suddenly found Chen Guiliang detestable.

Some netizens didn't just curse in the comment sections of the public intellectuals' blogs; they even followed Chen Guiliang to his personal accounts on Xiaonei and Hainei to bombard him with insults.

Chen Guiliang had no choice but to post a response: "In view of the doubts raised by some public intellectuals and netizens, I will explain the basic situation point by point..."

"First, some say I interfere with freedom of speech by arbitrarily deleting articles. Xiaonei and Hainei have strict review standards, which everyone, including myself, must abide by. Many accounts have been warned by editors, but bans and deletions are not used lightly. If an article is deleted, it's either because it has been proven to be a rumor or a particularly malicious personal attack. The author of that article has already broken the law!"

"Second, when the development of *Age of the Future* began, *DNF* hadn't even been officially released. Did I send commercial spies to Korea to plagiarize it?"

"Third, some say the development of *Age of the Future* is too slow precisely because we realized halfway through that the game was not good. They claim we deleted the previous year's content and then went to copy *DNF*. This claim shows a good imagination, but I really can't explain it."

"Fourth, even if my company's developers drew inspiration from Korea's *DNF*, how can one determine if it's plagiarism? The game's world-building, plot, characters, graphics... are all completely different. May I ask what exactly I plagiarized?"

"Some say I copied the core gameplay. How ridiculous is that statement? It's like a director being the first to make a martial arts film. Then you say all subsequent martial arts films are plagiarism because the core and form are the same."

"Fifth, I don't think netizens who haven't played the game themselves have any right to make any comments. You can't just rely on your imagination, or on having read someone's article, to decide that my company's game is a copy."

"Sixth, early next month, *Age of the Future* will be updated with its second chapter. At that time, 2,000 invitation codes will be distributed. If you want to criticize me, please play my game first. Go fill out the application for an invitation code now."

Chen Guiliang didn't write this response with the intention of convincing everyone.

Because it was impossible to convince them; they were already biased.

Chen Guiliang was just taking the opportunity to advertise, and incidentally convince those who were slightly more rational.

Next, he had to hire people and form a professional public relations team. They would argue with the haters online on one hand, and promote the game during the arguments on the other.

As the person involved, nothing Chen Guiliang said would be useful.

He needed the PR team or paid posters to pretend to be ordinary netizens and argue with the haters. And they had to present solid evidence to convince the neutral netizens who were just watching the show.

Of course, Chen Guiliang would definitely retaliate against the public intellectuals who had slandered him. But not now. He had to wait for public opinion to die down, otherwise, a rash counterattack would only make things worse.

What he could do now was to collect their past statements, pick out the most outrageous parts, and release them all at once after some time.

As it turned in, Chen Guiliang had a huge number of online fans.

When the newly formed PR team hired paid posters to argue with the haters, they posted side-by-side screenshots of *Age of the Future* and *DNF*. They also posted other details about the two games. Soon, Chen Guiliang's fans, armed with this information and screenshots, spontaneously went to argue with the haters.

"Besides the gameplay, are there any similarities between these two games? Why don't you say *DNF* copied *Double Dragon*?"

"*Double Dragon* is a Famicom game. Your example is not valid."

"By your logic, all current MMOs, including *World of Warcraft*, are copies. Because their core gameplay was established more than twenty years ago. It's just that they were purely text-based games back then."

"*World of Warcraft* couldn't possibly be a copy, because it created a real and grand virtual world."

"Heh, according to you, having the same gameplay is considered plagiarism. Well, not to mention anything else, the dungeons in *World of Warcraft* are copied, because games had dungeons before it."

"Dungeons are a reasonable use of inspiration."

"??? So *Age of the Future* is plagiarism, but *World of Warcraft* is just inspiration, is that it?"

Similar arguments could often be seen on major forums and Tieba.

The vast crowd of onlookers came to watch the spectacle. Anyone with a brain could see who was right and who was wrong. Because the haters were applying such obvious double standards.

To put it more bluntly, even if Chen Guiliang hadn't been reborn, *Age of the Future* could not be considered plagiarism.

Otherwise, *World of Warcraft* and *Black Myth: Wukong* would all be copies too.

Amidst these heated debates, two things happened.

First, *Age of the Future* was updated with its second chapter, and an additional 2,000 closed beta invitation codes were released.

Second, some traditional media outlets entered the fray, starting to reprint and comment on those slanderous articles. Needless to say, the Koreans' follow-up had arrived.

Chen Guiliang wasn't angry; instead, he joked, "The mastermind behind this is not very impressive. No major newspapers are involved. If they could get the *Southern Metropolis Daily* or the *Beijing News* to make a move, then I'd be impressed by their capabilities."

Chi Siyuan, the editor-in-chief of Hainei, who used to work for a traditional newspaper, said with a smile, "It's probably because they didn't pay enough. Newspapers have a gray income source called cooperation fees, also known as 'story-killing fees.' You pay the newspaper not to publish negative articles."

"Just killing a story can cost anywhere from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of yuan. To bribe the *Southern Metropolis Daily* to run a negative report, one article would cost at least 500,000 yuan. The *Beijing News* might be two or three hundred thousand. And even if the *Southern Metropolis Daily* and the *Beijing News* took the money, the negative content would be written very subtly. Being unsubtle could lead to trouble."

"Unless it can significantly boost newspaper sales, or if they're paid a huge amount at once, no newspaper will accept money to publish a hit piece. Third-rate tabloids are an exception."

The ones slandering *Age of the Future* this time were indeed third-rate tabloids.

It was unclear whether the Koreans were being cheap or if the people carrying it out had skimmed off the top, but in any case, only third-rate newspapers came forward.

The newspapers didn't make much of a splash, but the update to *Age of the Future* was a sensation.

This time, 2,000 additional closed beta invitation codes were released, of which more than 200 were given to editors of gaming websites and magazines.

When those editors played it for themselves, they were instantly captivated by the game's content.

Besides the graphics and playability, the game's plot was also a breath of fresh air for them.

In this era, post-apocalyptic themes already existed, but spiritual qi revival was unheard of.

The Eastern-style classes detailed within, and the class advancement quests updated this time, were all related to spiritual qi revival.

Gaming-related media outlets unanimously published articles praising *Age of the Future*.

Other game companies were on high alert. Another game was coming to take a piece of their pie!

Korea.

Seo Min asked, "Has the reputation of *Age of the Future* been ruined? Have any Chinese companies restarted negotiations with us?"

"No companies have restarted negotiations yet," said the executive in charge of overseas affairs, holding up printed newspapers and online articles. "These are all the negative reports and online comments about *Age of the Future*. I've had them translated into Korean."

Seo Min nodded in approval, then asked, "What kind of newspaper is this *The Economic Observer · Local Business Information*?"

The executive said, "It's a publication under the Shandong Press Group in China, very influential there."

In reality, this was all nonsense.

This newspaper was using the name of a legitimate publication, and its main source of profit was collecting "publicity fees" from small and medium-sized enterprises. To put it bluntly, it was extortion, threatening to publish negative news if they weren't paid.

There were many such illegal tabloids in the 2000s; a little money was all it took to get them to publish an article.

If the Korean side's implementers hadn't posted photos of the newspaper online, Chen Guiliang wouldn't have even seen the relevant content. Because its circulation was pathetically small, and even illegally distributed, you couldn't necessarily buy it even if you wanted to.

How could Seo Min understand any of this? He thought his plan had succeeded.

The money he allocated for the job was little to begin with, and the planners and implementers had to take their cuts at two levels. Bribing a few tabloids to fool him was already quite something.

If Seo Min had really dared to allocate millions, the *Southern Metropolis Daily* and the *Beijing News* would probably have cooperated.

Only certain public intellectuals, because it was difficult to monetize their traffic at the time, would dare to curse even the Jade Emperor for just a thousand or two yuan.

Seo Min waited and waited, but still no major companies came to restart negotiations.

Instead, some Chinese companies that previously hadn't been qualified to enter the bidding, seeing that *Age of the Future* seemed poised to be a huge hit, came to the Koreans to discuss licensing *DNF*.

They wanted to spend a small amount of money to import *DNF* and then launch it to ride the coattails of *Age of the Future*'s popularity.

*DNF*, the real Captain Li Kui, had become the impostor Li Gui, and now it had to piggyback on *Age of the Future*'s hype.

This whole situation made Seo Min furious. From a pile of small and medium-sized companies, he picked a relatively legitimate one to save face.

That company had quite a background; it was "ChinaVision," a subsidiary of CCTV.

Yes, the seemingly upright CCTV was also involved in the online gaming industry... and had already licensed two games, *Fantasia Sango 2* and *Gundam Online*.

It was even the exclusive distributor in China for EA, UBI, and KOEI!

The *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* series, the *FIFA* series, the *Dynasty Warriors* series, *Spore*, *SimCity*, and other single-player games were later also distributed by this company.

Who knows if the Koreans and CCTV would have a pleasant partnership.
